Comanche

Comanche people’s histories connect the Southern Plains, Texas and the present Comanche Nation in Oklahoma. This foundation brings the Nation’s own account together with community-directed language history, a consulted Texas report, an edited treaty and attributed educational accounts. Historical bands, the broader people and the present government retain their own contexts.

A source guide for a deeper dive.This entry provides a brief orientation and an organized reading path. A comprehensive deep dive has not yet been completed. Follow the annotated sources and distinguish primary community accounts from outside reference material.
Still unfinished

One selected museum educational work strengthens twentieth-century language and individual community-continuity coverage. Ten substantive works still have selected/mediated evidence and uneven historical coverage; original school/military records, fuller community and government histories, and more Comanche-authored scholarship remain unreviewed. Quantity does not establish adequacy, completion or endorsement.

Assessment recorded October 27, 2026. This is separate from research completion and community review.

  • Selected-page and selected-section review does not imply complete reading of each volume.
  • Underlying treaty manuscript, negotiations, implementation and later legal interpretation remain unreviewed.
  • TxDOT internal chronology and evaluative interpretations require comparison rather than automatic adoption.
  • The 1999 education record is historical; current program outcomes and language-use counts are not verified.
  • No community review or endorsement is recorded.
  • The 1844 text is an edited English archival transcription with OCR/signatory-layout limits. Original manuscript, translation, ratification and implementation need separate review.
  • The 1847 study is outside scholarly interpretation, substantially mediated by settler records. Its two internally problematic date statements are excluded.
  • The Nation’s remembrance article supplies named experiences but no verified publication year or complete military-history evidence. It is not a program-outcome assessment.
  • Comanche-authored historical scholarship and distinct band-level histories remain important gaps. Treaty participation alone does not establish every community’s consent or present citizenship.
  • The Smithsonian addition reviews selected edited Chibitty passages, not full interviews, original school/military records or comprehensive twentieth-century community/government history. A daughter’s statement is read through the museum’s citation to Williams (2005), not through independent review of that article.
Backdrop images & credits

These images have individual, documented connections to this entry. Their captions and source records define the people, place, object, and period shown; no one image represents every community within a broader label.

Comanche Village, Women Dressing Robes and Drying Meat, 1834–1835
George Catlin, 1834–1835. Smithsonian American Art Museum, Gift of Mrs. Joseph Harrison, Jr., 1985.66.346. Public domain.

Source & image record ↗ · Public domain — SAAM item marked Free to use

Smithsonian American Art Museum identifies this George Catlin oil painting specifically as a Comanche village and gives its date as 1834–1835. Its description attributes the 1834 village sketch and the foreground work interpretation to Catlin. This is an outside artist’s historical representation, not a documentary photograph, Comanche-made artwork, a present government depiction, or evidence that every Comanche community lived or worked identically. No exact present-state location, village name, named individual, current cultural practice or territorial boundary is inferred from the scene. Catlin’s quoted village-size claims and stereotypes are not adopted. Complete 3000x1979 delivered museum source JPEG preserved. Proposed web copy resized proportionally to 1800x1187 and recompressed at JPEG quality 88; no pixel crop, retouching, recoloring, generated content or added detail. Card/page CSS crops and overlays must be disclosed. CSS may crop or overlay directory/background copies; the opened-page image preserves the complete delivered source frame.

Start reading here

Comanche people, historical bands and the present Oklahoma-based Comanche Nation retain distinct scopes. The TxDOT review covers selected pages, and the NMAI path covers selected text sections rather than a complete exhibition or interview; no audio was evaluated. Automated retrieval failures do not establish a reader paywall.

  1. History — the Comanche Nation’s institutional account

    The Comanche Nation's brief history introduces movement and kinship-based bands in the government's own voice.

  2. TxDOT Tribal Histories: Comanche Nation Research Report — selected pages

    Selected pages of this report add Texas chronology with documented Nation preservation-office consultation; its internal date problems remain flagged.

  3. About Us — Comanche Nation Language Department

    The Language Department explains how community planning and preservation work led to its stated teaching goals.

  4. Native Words, Native Warriors — Charles Chibitty’s schooling, wartime language work and later life

    Selected Charles Chibitty material connects schooling, wartime language work and later teaching through clearly attributed individual and family recollections.

These are selected starting points. The full annotated collection, source perspectives, inspection limits and remaining research questions follow below. A starting guide is not an exhaustive history or community endorsement.

01

Names, a wider people and a present Nation

The Comanche Nation uses Nʉmʉnʉʉ for its people. Its own historical account connects movement onto the Plains with horse-based life and kinship-based bands. This people-level directory route and the present government are related levels of description, rather than one unchanged organization across all periods. Current membership numbers and governing rules require separate dated verification.

Read the sources [1] Comanche Nation

02

Bands need their own context

The consulted TxDOT report describes changing local bands and wider divisions, with relationships that could form and change. Penateka, Nokoni and Quahadi are among its historical labels. These names should remain individually searchable when their identities and aliases are checked; a list of bands does not prove that each is a separate present government.

Read the sources [5] Texas Department of Transportation

03

Plains movement and Texas history

The Nation’s account follows movement southward and emphasizes horses and bison. TxDOT’s selected historical chapters connect Texas history to military pressure and removal to reservation life. These broad accounts provide a starting chronology, not precise homeland boundaries. The report contains internal date problems that remain disclosed in its source card.

Read the sources [1] Comanche Nation [5] Texas Department of Transportation

04

Reading the 1867 treaty critically

The Medicine Lodge treaty transcription contains a reservation provision, a reserved hunting clause and a consent requirement for later cession of reservation land. It also sets out federal services and compulsory English-school attendance. The text places promises of protection and services alongside compulsory schooling and requirements to make the reservation a permanent home. The wording alone does not establish implementation, universal agreement or present-day legal rights.

Read the sources [6] Oklahoma State University Libraries, Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties

05

Community-directed language institutions

The Language Department’s account traces its planning to community organizing in 2017 and funding for fiscal 2019. It recognizes the earlier preservation committee and describes teacher certification, curriculum and digital resources among its goals. These are the department’s reported history and aims; this review did not test an app, inspect a curriculum or measure fluency.

Read the sources [4] Comanche Nation Language Department

06

A dated record of teaching across communities

Fuentes’s 1999 source book records preservation work and a Toya Band language class in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. It describes volunteer teaching, intergenerational participation and materials in that historical setting. The two program entries form one reviewed educational work. They do not establish today’s schedule, participation or separate-government status.

Read the sources [7] Southwest Educational Development Laboratory; ERIC, U.S. Department of Education

07

Language, family memory and individual experience

The Boulder report presents Ruth Toathy’s and Rosemary Chibity’s differing memories of language use at home and pressure toward English, alongside Leonard Chibity’s comments on place names. These are named personal accounts within an edited public report. They help readers see lived experiences without turning one recollection into a statement about every Comanche family.

Read the sources [8] City of Boulder, with named Comanche contributors

08

A Texas primary document before Medicine Lodge

The 1844 Tehuacana Creek text joins peace provisions with regulated trade, government agents and proposed English-language, Christian and agricultural instruction. Its 22 articles make those different aims visible together. The document lists several Indigenous parties separately; a shared instrument does not merge their identities. References to a line do not themselves establish a precise agreed territorial boundary.

Read the sources [9] Texas State Library archival edition; later Texas State Historical Association reprint; Texas History Trust digital reading copy

09

Penateka diplomacy and German settlement

Babcock’s study of the 1847 Meusebach agreement gives Comanche leaders and intermediaries a role alongside the German negotiator. He challenges accounts that credit one man alone and places negotiations within settlement pressures. His interpretation is useful to compare with the primary record; it should not become a claim that every Comanche band accepted the same agreement or that later pressures disappeared.

Read the sources [10] Yearbook of German-American Studies / Society for German-American Studies; University of Kansas journal platform

10

Remembering code talkers through families and language

In the Nation’s report, Lloyd Heminokeky explains the importance of honoring code talkers through family participation and language-department work. LaNora Parker describes her father Simmons Parker as a teacher of Comanche history and pride. These named accounts connect public remembrance with family learning, without defining every family’s experience or reproducing songs and ceremonial material.

Read the sources [11] Comanche Nation, Communications

11

Schooling and wartime language use in one person’s account

The museum places Charles Chibitty’s recollection in his Ft. Sill Indian School years: he and his cousin stopped speaking their language when staff approached. Its text distinguishes this from Haskell, where it says Native languages were allowed despite strict discipline. The same resource presents his memories of Comanche military recruitment and collaborative code-making. These are selected, edited recollections, not a record of every school, speaker or military unit.

Read the sources [12] National Museum of the American Indian, Smithsonian Institution

12

A veteran’s later working and teaching life

The exhibition follows Chibitty beyond military service into further education, work as a glazier and continued community life. It cites his adopted daughter Carrie Wilson’s memory of his readiness to teach Comanche, through a 2005 article by Rudi Williams. This is an attributed family account in the museum’s retelling; the original article and complete interview were not independently reviewed. It offers an individual example of continuity rather than a measure of language-program success.

Read the sources [12] National Museum of the American Indian, Smithsonian Institution

13

What this foundation still needs

Ten inspected works now offer a wider reading foundation, including Texas diplomacy and selected twentieth-century experiences of schooling, military language work and later teaching. Comanche-authored historical scholarship, original negotiation and implementation records, fuller community and government histories, and careful band-level comparisons remain needed. A selected personal account does not fill all those gaps. No comprehensive history, current legal assessment or community endorsement is claimed.

Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, 1867 — edited primary text ↗

Treaty with the Kiowa and Comanche, October 21, 1867, 15 Stat. 581; ratification advised July 25, 1868; proclaimed August 25, 1868. Edited text, Oklahoma State University Libraries.

Publication: 1867-10-21

The edited treaty text juxtaposes reservation and hunting provisions with federal promises and compulsory schooling. Its wording is evidence of the agreement’s terms, not proof of implementation or every Comanche person’s consent.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual HTML preamble, ratification/proclamation metadata, Articles1–16 and signatory columns; selected focus Articles2,7,11,12,16. Manuscript, scan images, negotiations, ratification record and subsequent interpretation not independently inspected.

Review recorded: October 26, 2026

Native Words, Native Warriors — Charles Chibitty’s schooling, wartime language work and later life ↗

National Museum of the American Indian. Native Words, Native Warriors. Smithsonian Institution, copyright 2020. Selected sections 3.5, Comanche excerpts in 4.2 and 4.4, and 6.3; credits identify Edwin Schupman as project developer and writer and NMAI 2004 code-talker interviews.

Selected Charles Chibitty material connects schooling, wartime language work and later teaching. The resource distinguishes his recollections, family testimony and museum narration; it is one educational work, not a count per chapter or speaker.

Inspection: Content reviewed for the stated scope

Scope: Actual public HTML: Chapter 3 opening and section 3.5 (web lines 97–110); Chapter 4 Comanche recruitment passage and Chibitty excerpt (lines 63–64, 88–92) and Creating Special Code Words with his account (lines 146–156); Chapter 6 section 6.3 (lines 77–84). Introduction 1.4 and Chapter 2 Comanche orientation were read for identification/context, not counted separately. Actual credits lines 9–20, 70–117 identify production, writer and interview/recording provenance. No complete exhibition, interview, audio, classroom worksheet, code dictionary, image or map inspection claimed.

Review recorded: October 27, 2026

Access status: Public readable English HTML, no login/paywall encountered

Access note: Reading was of text and captions, not audio playback or pictures. Section 3.5 distinguishes Ft. Sill punishment from Haskell, where the museum says Native languages were allowed despite strict discipline. Do not flatten those schools into one identical policy. Section 6.3 attributes daughter Carrie Wilson’s statement through Rudi Williams (2005); the underlying article was not independently inspected. Whole interviews, school files and military records remain unreviewed. No current speaker/membership totals, hereditary-leadership generalization or program-outcome claim is adopted. Web extraction of the actual HTML body succeeded; normal Python direct retrieval returned HTTP403 for all four selected/credit URLs. No retry, access-control bypass or reader-paywall inference was made. The actual web-tool body response is retained privately.
